source_text: Hac sunt doctrinae hominum et daemoniorum, prurientibus auribus natae de ingenio sapientise saecularis, quam dominus stultitiam vocans stulta mundi in confusionem etiam philosophiae ipsius elegit. Ea est enim materia sapientiae saecularis, temeraria interpres divinae naturae et dispositionis. Ipsae denique haereses a philosophia subornantur. Inde aeones, et formae nescio quae infinitae, et trinitas hominis apud Valentinum; Platonicus fuerat: inde Marcionis deus melior de tranquillitate; a Stoicis venerat: et ut anima interire dicatur, ab Epicureis observatur: et ut carnis restitutio negetur, de una omnium philosophorum schola sumitur: et ubi materia cum deo aequatur, Zenonis disciplina est: et ubi aliquid de igneo deo allegatur, Heracletus intervenit. Eadem materia apud haereticos et philosophos volutatur, idem retractatus implicantur: unde malum, et quare? et unde homo, et quomodo? et, quod proxime Valentinus proposuit, unde deus? scilicet de enthymesi et ectromate. Miserum Aristotelem! qui illis dialecticam instituit, artificem struendi et destruendi, versipellem in sententiis, coactam in coniecturis, duram in argumentis, operariam contentionum, molestam etiam sibi ipsi, omnia retractantem, ne quid omnino tractaverit. Hinc illae fabulae et genealogiae interminabiles, et quaestiones infructuosae, et sermones serpentes velut cancer, a quibus nos apostolus refrenans nominatim philosophiam contestatur caveri oportere, scribens ad Colossenses, Videte, ne qui sit circumveniens vos per philosophiam et inanem seductionem, secundum traditionem hominum, praeter providentiam spiritus sancti. Fuerat Athenis, et istam sapientiam humanam, affectatricem et interpolatricem veritatis, de congressibus noverat, ipsam quoque in suas haereses multipartitam varietate sectarum invicem repugnantium. Quid ergo Athenis et Hierosolymis? quid academiae et ecclesiae? quid haereticis et Christianis? Nostra institutio de porticu Solomonis est, qui et ipse tradiderat dominum in simplicitate cordis esse quaerendum. Viderint qui Stoicum et Platonicum et dialecticum Christianismum protulerunt. Nobis curiositate opus non est post Christum Iesum, nec inquisitione post evangelium. Cum credimus, nihil desideramus ultra credere. Hoc enim prius credimus, non esse quod ultra credere debeamus.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that heretical teachings derive from pagan philosophy, not from the apostolic tradition.
pass_a_gloss: These are doctrines of men and of demons, born for itching ears from the talent of worldly wisdom, which the Lord, calling it foolishness, chose the foolish things of the world for the confusion even of philosophy itself. For that is the material of worldly wisdom, a rash interpreter of the divine nature and arrangement. In short, the heresies themselves are equipped from philosophy. From there come aeons, and I know not what infinite forms, and the trinity of man in Valentinus; he had been a Platonist. From there comes the better god of Marcion, from tranquility; he had come from the Stoics. And that the soul is said to perish is taken from the Epicureans. And that the restoration of the flesh is denied is taken from the one school of all the philosophers. And where matter is made equal with God, it is the teaching of Zeno. And where something about a fiery god is alleged, Heraclitus intervenes. The same material is rolled over among heretics and philosophers, the same retracings are entangled: whence is evil, and why? and whence is man, and how? and, what Valentinus most recently proposed, whence is God? evidently from enthymesis and ectroma. Wretched Aristotle! who established dialectic for them, the artisan of building and destroying, changeable in opinions, forced in conjectures, harsh in arguments, a worker of contentions, troublesome even to himself, retracting everything, lest he should have treated anything at all. From there come those fables and endless genealogies, and fruitless questions, and speeches creeping like cancer, from which the apostle, restraining us, testifies by name that philosophy must be guarded against, writing to the Colossians: See that no one is deceiving you through philosophy and empty seduction, according to the tradition of men, contrary to the providence of the Holy Spirit. He had been at Athens, and he had known that human wisdom, the imitator and corrupter of truth, from his encounters, and he knew it also divided into its own heresies by the variety of sects mutually fighting. What then is there between Athens and Jerusalem? what between the academy and the church? what between heretics and Christians? Our instruction is from the porch of Solomon, who himself had also handed down that the Lord must be sought in simplicity of heart. Let them see to it who have produced a Stoic and Platonic and dialectic Christianity. For us there is no need of curiosity after Christ Jesus, nor of inquiry after the gospel. When we believe, we desire nothing beyond to believe. For this we believe first, that there is nothing which we ought to believe beyond.

choices.why: The glossary bans 'worldly wisdom' for philosophia, but this is a different phrase; 'worldly wisdom' captures the contrast with divine wisdom that Tertullian is drawing.
The verb means to supply or furnish secretly; 'equipped' conveys that philosophy provides the resources for heresies without implying direct causation.
Temeraria means reckless or presumptuous; 'rash' captures the accusation that philosophy oversteps its bounds in explaining divine things.
The word literally means 'skin-changing' and implies shifting or two-faced; 'changeable' fits the context of dialectic's shifting arguments.

choices.english: the imitator and corrupter of truth
choices.why: Affectatrix means one who strives after or imitates; interpolatrix means one who tampers with or corrupts. The pair captures the double accusation against philosophy.
rejected: the pretender and falsifier of truth
the rival and adulterator of truth

choices.why: Porticus is the colonnade or porch; Tertullian contrasts the academy with Solomon's porch, the place of apostolic teaching in Acts.

bible_refs.note: Videte, ne qui sit circumveniens vos per philosophiam et inanem seductionem, secundum traditionem hominum, praeter providentiam spiritus sancti

pass_b_english: These are the doctrines of men and demons, born for itching ears from the cleverness of philosophy, which the Lord calls foolishness and chose the foolish things of the world to confound even philosophy itself (1 Corinthians 1:27). For that is the material of philosophy: a presumptuous interpreter of the divine nature and order. The heresies themselves are equipped by philosophy. From there come the aeons and the infinite forms, whatever they are, and the trinity of man in Valentinus; he had been a Platonist. From there comes Marcion's better god, from tranquility; he had come from the Stoics. And when it is said that the soul dies, that is taken from the Epicureans. And when the restoration of the flesh is denied, that is drawn from the single school of all the philosophers. And where matter is made equal with God, that is the teaching of Zeno. And where something about a fiery god is alleged, Heraclitus steps in. The same material is rolled over among heretics and philosophers; the same retracings entangle them: where does evil come from, and why? And where does man come from, and how? And, what Valentinus recently proposed, where does God come from? From enthymesis and ectroma, of course. Wretched Aristotle! He set up dialectic for them, the craftsman of building and destroying, changeable in opinions, forced in conjectures, harsh in arguments, a worker of contentions, troublesome even to himself, retracting everything so that he might treat nothing at all. From there come those fables and endless genealogies, and fruitless questions, and words creeping like cancer, from which the apostle restrains us and testifies by name that philosophy must be avoided, writing to the Colossians: See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition, apart from the providence of the Holy Spirit (Colossians 2:8). He had been at Athens, and he knew that human wisdom, the imitator and corrupter of truth, from his encounters there, was itself divided into its own heresies by the variety of mutually opposing schools. What then does Athens have to do with Jerusalem? What does the academy have to do with the church? What do heretics have to do with Christians? Our instruction is from the porch of Solomon, who himself had handed down that the Lord must be sought in simplicity of heart. Let those who have produced a Stoic and Platonic and dialectic Christianity see to it. We have no need of curiosity after Jesus Christ, nor of inquiry after the gospel. When we believe, we desire nothing beyond belief. For this we believe first: that there is nothing beyond which we ought to believe.

problems.why: lint glossary: banned rendering of philosophia; use 'philosophy' ('worldly wisdom')

edits.old: born for itching ears from the cleverness of worldly wisdom
edits.new: born for itching ears from the cleverness of philosophy

edits.old: For that is the material of worldly wisdom:
edits.new: For that is the material of philosophy:

fixed: The source 'sapientiae saecularis' is rendered 'worldly wisdom' in two places, but the glossary bans 'worldly wisdom' for 'philosophia' and requires 'philosophy'. The source phrase 'sapientiae saecularis' is the Latin for 'worldly wisdom' (literally 'wisdom of the age'), but the glossary entry for 'philosophia' bans 'worldly wisdom' and requires 'philosophy'. The first instance 'de ingenio sapientise saecularis' is rendered 'from the cleverness of worldly wisdom' and the second 'Ea est enim materia sapientiae saecularis' is rendered 'For that is the material of worldly wisdom'. Both should use 'philosophy' instead of 'worldly wisdom' to comply with the glossary.

problems.quote: a rash interpreter of the divine nature and order.
problems.why: 'Rash interpreter' is odd; likely means 'presumptuous' or 'bold' interpreter, not hasty.
problems.fix: Use 'presumptuous interpreter of the divine nature and order.'

edits.old: a rash interpreter of the divine nature and order.
edits.new: a presumptuous interpreter of the divine nature and order.

fixed: Changed 'rash' to 'presumptuous' for 'temeraria' (bold, presumptuous, reckless), which better captures the sense of overstepping bounds in interpreting divine things.
